STATEMENT OF THE CASE
Legal Background
 In Defendant’s Answer to the Amended
Complaint, Defendant expressly stated that Plaintiff
Jasmine Younge was a member of the district
attorney’s personal staff. [ECF No. 53 at 10]. This
term of art— “personal staff” — is the precise
statutory language used in Title VII of the Civil
Rights Act of 1964. 42. U.S.C. § 2000e(f).

 In the context of Rule 8, this Court has
repeatedly stated that the initial pleadings serve to
provide “fair notice” to the parties of the claims and
defenses relied on, if the notice is sufficiently factual
to impart that notice. The Answer invoked the
statutory language used in Title VII to describe those
employees who are not covered by the statute. The
admission was express and unequivocal. When the
Defendant clearly admitted that the Plaintiff was a
member of the district attorney’s personal staff,
invoking Title VII’s specific term of art, it was
sufficient to provide fair notice that the defense may
rely on that admitted fact in its defense.

 Beyond invoking the defense in the Answer,
Defendant’s counsel stated in a March 2022 discovery
hearing before the district judge that the defense was
relying on the personal staff exception. Counsel for
Plaintiff did not object nor request any additional
discovery on this issue. Further, after raising the
defense in its motion for summary judgment, the
magistrate assigned to the case offered to reopen
discovery if there was any relevant issue on the
personal staff exception the Plaintiff wanted to

2

explore: counsel could not articulate any additional
discovery that was needed. Even ignoring the notice
of the intent to rely on Younge’s status as a member
of the district attorney’s personal staff in the Answer,
Plaintiff was not remotely prejudiced by the district
court and Court of Appeals deciding the case on the
merits rather than a technicality.

 Because the Petition does not account for the
Answer in which the defense expressly provided
notice that Younge was part of the district attorney’s
personal staff, the arguments within the Petition are
inapplicable to this case.

Factual Background
Plaintiff worked at th e District Attorney’s
Office for about two months in 2019 as then-District
Attorney Paul Howard Jr.’s Deputy Chief of Staff and
Director of Programs. [Pet. App’x 33a]. She was paid
more than the attorneys empl oyed by the Office, and
only the district attorney was paid more. Her large
salary was only made possible because she was a
member of Howard’s personal staff. [ Id.]. To obtain
the funding for her position, Howard had to execute
an Official Oath in Support of Hiring Personal Staff.
In the Oath, he swore that he had “reviewed the
definition of personal staff” contained in Fulton
County’s policies and that he intended to hire Younge
“to be a member of his personal staff.” The signed
Oath was placed in Younge’s personnel file. [Id.].

Plaintiff testified that she reported only to
Howard, that she was with him constantly, that her
schedule was “pretty much the schedule that DA Paul
Howard had,” and that she was involved with “pretty

3

much everything” that had to do with the District
Attorney’s Office. [Id. at 35a].

Howard testified that in late June or early July,
after numerous complaints were made about Younge
by long-tenured staff and after he overheard Younge
berating an attorney from the Major Crimes Division
in the hallway outside his office, he told Younge that
she was not working out and that he intended to
terminate her. [ECF. No. 104-4]. A day or two later,
Howard found a letter on his desk from Younge
stating that she was preg nant. He later terminated
her employment as he had told her he would.
REASONS FOR DENYING THE PETITION-
I. THE PERSONAL STAFF DEFENSE WAS
ADEQUATELY PLEAD IN DEFENDANT’S
ANSWER TO THE AMENDED COMPLAINT.

Petitioner Younge seeks a decision from this
Court to prevent a defendant from raising an
affirmative defense in a motion for summary
judgment—even where there is no prejudice to a
plaintiff—when it has not been plead in a defendant’s
answer. This petition is the first time that Respondent
has understood Petitioner to assert that the “personal
staff” defense was never invoked prior to the motion
for summary judgment. In fact, Respondent
affirmatively and unequivocally stated in its Answer
that Petitioner was a member of the district attorney’s
personal staff, and raised it numerous times, both in
hearings before the district court and in discovery
responses. [ECF No. 53 at 10].

4

Beyond Title VII’s precise term of art, “personal
staff,” being expressly relied on in the Answer, the
defense was specifically discussed at a hearing before
the district court, prior to the close of discovery and
filing of the motion for summary judgment. Petitioner
did not object nor request additional discovery. And
even after the motion for summary judgment was
filed, the district court provided Petitioner with the
option to reopen discovery on the topic. But Petitioner
could not articulate any further discovery she believed
was needed on the issue.

In her Amended Complaint, Petitioner alleged
that she was told by a staff member at Fulton
County’s human resources department that she was a
member of the district attorney’s executive staff. In
fact, the Petitioner was compensated with the secondhighest salary at the district attorney’s office, behind
only the district attorney. The ability to pay Petitioner
such a high salary was because the district attorney
signed an “Official Oath in Support of Hiring Personal
Staff” swearing that Petitioner would serve as “a
member of his personal staff.” [Pet. App’x 33a]. This
Oath permitted the district attorney to pay Petitioner
a salary significantly higher than that of other
employees, including attorneys.

In response to this allegation in the Amended
Complaint, Respondent “admit[ted] that as Deputy
Chief of Staff to the District Attorney[,] Plaintiff was
a member of the District Attorney’s…personal staff.”
[ECF No. 53 at 10]. In so doing, Respondent
affirmatively stated that Petitioner was a member of
the district attorney’s personal staff—the precise
term used in Title VII to describe the “exception.”

5


Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(b)(1)(A) requires that defenses
be stated in “short and plain terms.” This Court has
repeatedly held in the co ntext of Rule 8 that the
practical importance of the initial pleadings is to
provide “fair notice” to the opposing party of the
defense’s assertions and set forth sufficient “factual
matter” to fairly impart that notice. See e.g., Bell Atl.
v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555-556 (2007). Expressly
admitting that the Petitioner was a member of the
district attorney’s personal staff—Title VII’s precise
term of art—plainly satisfies this standard.1 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000e(f).

It has long been this Court’s position that cases
should be decided on the merits rather than
procedural technicalities. “The Federal Rules reject
the approach that pleading is a game of skill in which
one misstep by counsel may be decisive to the outcome
and accept the principle that the purpose of pleading
is to facilitate a proper decision on the merits.” Foman
v. Davis , 371 U.S. 178, 181 (1962). The express
admission in the Answer that Petitioner was a
member of the district attorney’s “personal staff”
invoked Title VII’s statutory language and was more
than sufficient to provide “fair notice.”

This Petition’s support is built on a flawed
foundation that simply ignores the initial pleadings.
The “personal staff” defense was adequately raised in

1 Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(b) requires on ly that defenses be stated in a
numbered paragraph. This requirement was also satisfied by the
admission that Petitioner was a member of the district attorney’s
personal staff.

6

the Answer. The express admission that Petitioner
was a member of the district attorney’s “personal
staff” provided fair notice that the Defendant may rely
on a term of art defined in  the very statute that
Petitioner chose to bring suit under. The factual
circumstance that the Petition is premised on is not
found in this case.

CONCLUSION

Petitioner Jasmine Younge has sought review
of a decision of the district  court and the Eleventh
Circuit Court of Appeals. Petitioner asserts that the
personal staff exception was never raised prior to the
submission of the motion for summary judgment. In
fact, Respondent District Attorney’s Office provided
express and unequivocal notice in its Answer that
Younge was a member of the district attorney’s
personal staff.

Because the Petition asks this Court to accept
this case based on a misstatement concerning the
notice provided in the initial pleadings and by counsel
in hearings before the district court prior to the
submission of the motion for summary judgment, and
because it is the established position of this Court to
construe pleadings to facilitate decisions on the merits
rather than technicalities, the Court should deny the
Petition.
